description: Tidemark built Bhoomi (bhoomi.earth):an AI guide that answers“Is this really changing where I live?” from NASA and NOAA records. Pick a place on the map or just ask, by text or voice, and Bhoomi tests the sea level,heat,rain or water-on-land record for a real trend (Mann-Kendall with Sen’s slope, seasons removed), gives a plain risk level and recommendation, and names every source. It also plugs into the AI assistant you already use (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot) with one address: bhoomi.earth/mcp/.
summary: Bhoomi (bhoomi.earth) answers one question for any place: is this really changing here? Pick a place on the map or just ask, by text or voice, in English, Hindi or Telugu. Bhoomi pulls the monthly record from public NASA and NOAA data (sea level at tide gauges worldwide, air temperature, the hottest day of each month, rain, and water stored on land from NASA's GRACE satellites), removes the seasons, and runs a real significance test (Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope, adjusted for autocorrelation). It answers rising, falling or no clear change, with the size of the change, a 95% range and the source. Code, not the AI, then turns the rate into a plain risk level against a published world average and a recommendation, for example for buying a home near the shore, with a clear note that it is based only on past records. When datasets disagree, it shows all of them; when there is no data, it says so, with no made-up number. The same tools plug into any AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot) at bhoomi.earth/mcp/. It is built for students, home buyers, investors and planners who need a local trend they can trust.
details:
What it does

Bhoomi helps everyday people check whether the climate where they live, build or invest is really changing, using measured records instead of guesses. Each measurement has its own window: sea level, air temperature, the hottest days, rain and water stored on land. Search for a town or tap the map (on Sea level the dots are real tide gauges), pin up to six places, and a recommendation card says what it means. For New York: "Moderate risk, +3.2 cm every 10 years, about as fast as the world average", what to check before buying near the shore, "+7.3 to +7.9 cm by 2050 if the past trend continues", and a note that this is based only on past records. A chart and a table compare the pinned places. For weather you can switch between NASA POWER, ERA5 and the nearest weather station and see whether they agree. An assistant on every window answers questions typed or spoken, in English, Hindi or Telugu.

How it works

  1. Pick or ask: choose a place and a measurement, or ask in plain words and the AI agent works out the place and what to measure.
  2. Fetch: three MCP tools (list_variables, get_series, detect_trend) pull a monthly record from a public dataset.
  3. Test: remove the seasonal cycle, then run the Mann-Kendall trend test with Sen's slope, adjusted for autocorrelation (Hamed-Rao). A trend is called only when p is below 0.05 and the whole 95% range sits on one side of zero; otherwise the answer is "no clear change".
  4. Answer: rising, falling or no clear change, with the rate per decade, the 95% range, the period and the source. The AI never does the maths; it is told to quote only numbers that came back from a tool.
  5. Guide: code, not the model, turns the rate into a risk level against a published reference (NASA's 3.4 mm a year world sea-level rise, NOAA's 0.20 °C per decade world warming), a recommendation, and an "if the past trend continues" range, shown only for records of 20 years or more and never called a forecast.
  6. Open: any MCP-capable AI assistant can use the same tools at https://bhoomi.earth/mcp/, with no key and no sign-in.

How we checked it

  • Atlantic City sea level: ours is +42.5 mm per decade (95% range 41.1 to 44.0); NOAA publishes 42.4 ± 0.8 mm per decade for the same tide gauge (station 8534720).
  • North-west India, Aug 2002 to Oct 2008: our GRACE land water fall is 5.3 cm of water a year (range 3.9 to 6.9); Rodell, Velicogna and Famiglietti (2009, Nature) report groundwater falling 4.0 ± 1.0 cm a year. The ranges overlap.
  • Statistics tests: pure noise, seasons only and autocorrelated noise all come back "no clear change", so it doesn't cry wolf.
  • Golden questions with answers set from NOAA and published papers, never from our own tool: the live agent passed 15 of 15 on Nov 15 at 1:00 AM and 11:20 AM EST. On the expanded 30-question set, the final build passed 27 of 30; the three misses were wording against our own style rules.

Honest limits

Grid datasets cover cells 25 to 50 km wide, not single streets. GRACE weighs all water on land and cannot separate groundwater from lakes and soil, and Bhoomi says so. Results describe the past; the future is not certain, and the guidance is not financial or legal advice.

Who it is for

Students checking a claim about their own town, families buying or building near the coast, investors comparing places, and planners asking whether heat or water shortage is really getting worse.

Tools and languages

Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, httpx and the MCP Python SDK (managed with uv); plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with MapLibre GL and OpenFreeMap tiles; hosted on Vercel. The in-app agent is Claude Haiku 5.5 through OpenRouter; the voice and chat assistant runs on ElevenLabs Agents; Langfuse traces every question and answer. About 1,350 pytest tests plus a golden-question eval suite. No accounts: saved places stay in the visitor's browser. Open source under Apache-2.0.

Live app: https://bhoomi.earth

dataRefs: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) monthly point data: air temperature, hottest day, rain
NASA GSFC GRACE and GRACE-FO mascons, RL06 v2.0: water stored on land
NASA Sea Level Change: world sea-level rise rate (our risk reference)
NASA IPCC AR6 Sea Level Projection Tool (linked for real projections)
projectRefs: ERA5 reanalysis (Copernicus/ECMWF) via the Open-Meteo historical archive
NOAA CO-OPS tide gauges (US sea level)
PSMSL tide gauges worldwide (Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level)
NOAA Climate.gov global temperature (our warming reference)
NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer (linked in recommendations)
FEMA Flood Map Service Center (linked in recommendations)
WRI Aqueduct water risk atlas (linked in recommendations)
Rodell, Velicogna and Famiglietti 2009, Nature (GRACE validation)
Loomis, Luthcke and Sabaka 2019, J. Geodesy (GRACE mascons)
Claude Code by Anthropic (AI coding assistant, SI)
Claude Haiku 5.5 through OpenRouter (in-app AI agent, SI)
ElevenLabs Agents (voice and chat assistant, AI-generated voice, SI)
OpenAI Codex CLI (drafted the demo video script, SI)
